newsitem.title: UK: BOE's George says UK inflation needs to be lower.
newsitem.headline: BOE's George says UK inflation needs to be lower.

text.p: Governor of the Bank of England Eddie George said on Wednesday Britain's monetary framework had yielded encouraging results, but the average rate of inflation over the last four years is not as low as it needs to be.
"The results over the past few years have, I would say, been encouraging, although it is still early days," he said in the text of the 1997 Barnett Lecture to be delivered at Toynbee Hall in London.
"Inflation over the past four years has in fact averaged about 2.75 percent which is not as low as it needs to be if we really are to squeeze inflationary expectations out of the system."
But George added that inflation has been lower, and for longer, than for a generation. "That in itself is a source of some satisfaction."
But he said more satisfying still was that the same period had seen relatively steady economic growth.
"All the forecasts expect that this combination of relatively low inflation and relatively stable growth will continue over the next two years."

The present monetary framework comprises an explicit 2.5 percent inflation target, quarterly inflation reports from the Bank, and monthly monetary meetings between the Bank and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.
It was established after the pound was forced out the Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992.

However, George said he felt the Bank still lacked public support. "There is a popular misconception that whenever there are signs of the economy just picking up, the Bank delights in calling for higher interest rates to drive it back on its knees."
He said he did not expect maintaining stability to be wildly popular, "but we do need public understanding of what we are trying to do and why we are trying to do it in order to be able to succeed."
